BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Come Monday, the second Pacific upper trough digging into the northwest region will bring another cold front across the area. The system will bring a 50-70% chance of light precipitation Monday through Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Continued warm and dry conditions Friday.
- Windy conditions on Friday ahead of a cold front.
- Valley rain and mountain snow along a cold front Friday night into Saturday morning.
- Cooler and unsettled pattern next week with snow levels lowering to valley floors by the end of the week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Strong southwest flow will continue considerably warmer than normal temperatures today, before a strong upper-level Pacific trough moves inland later today, driving a cold front eastward across the area. Windy conditions, with gusts 20-40 mph, will be expected this afternoon ahead of and along the frontal passage, with exposed areas in southeast OR and far southwest ID near NV border seeing gusts 35- 50 mph. The cold front will bring widespread precipitation throughout the area, with valleys seeing rain and higher terrain areas seeing snow showers tonight through Saturday morning. Snow levels will mostly linger in the 6000-8000 ft MSL range today, before gradually dropping into the 5000-7000 ft MSL range by early Saturday behind the frontal passage. As such, snow accumulations will continue to be limited to high mountain peaks. Precipitation will gradually taper off from west to east Saturday morning as the front pushes out of our area. Winds are expected to lower down to 5 to 15 mph for most areas by Saturday morning. Cooler temperatures will be expected Saturday behind the frontal passage.

A brief period of mostly dry conditions and temperatures 5 to 10 degrees above normal will be in store on Sunday, as our area stays under a dry but strong southwesterly flow ahead of another incoming Pacific trough. The dry break will be short lived, as precipitation chances return across eastern OR Sunday afternoon and evening, before spreading eastward into southwest ID late Sunday night. With snow levels mostly hanging in the 6000-7000 ft MSL range Sunday, light mountain snow showers and valley rain will be expected again with this second precipitation round.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Come Monday, the second Pacific upper trough digging into the northwest region will bring another cold front across the area. The system will bring a 50-70% chance of light precipitation Monday through Tuesday. Snow levels will drop down to 4000-6000 ft MSL by Tuesday, lowest across eastern Oregon. A brief dry period is expected early Wednesday morning before the next system moves in. This deep upper-level low will move overhead from mid to late week, bringing colder air than previous systems. Uncertainty remains over this system's exact pattern as it either digs across our area as an upper trough or dive down into the California coast as a closed upper low. For now, precipitation chances remain at 40-70% late Wednesday through Thursday, with temperatures favored to cool a few more degrees and snow levels around 3000-4500 feet. Come early Friday, our area is projected to be under a strong northerly flow as the upper low digs into the Desert Southwest region. Light remnant mountain snow showers are possible Friday, as snow levels are projected to drop down to valley floor levels by Friday.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Sunday is shaping up to be a mostly sunny autumn day with temperatures in the low to mid 50s for the Denver metro and east CO plains, which is near-average for the time of year.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will prevail today, followed by more seasonable temperatures this weekend into next week.
- Chances for rain and snow showers across the high country Saturday, with a few showers possible over the eastern plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Current satellite shows a clear night for much of the state with only a few thin high clouds over western CO. To our east, a much cooler airmass and its accompanying cold front have pushed over the Great Lakes and across the central Great Plains, up against our eastern counties. Given the clear skies in place, light easterly winds, and a somewhat of a surge in dewpoints (low to mid 30s), at least some patchy fog is likely over the eastern CO plains and along the South Platte River valley in the early morning hours. Areas of fog can already be seen slowly creeping over the CO-NE border. The fog should clear by mid morning as temperatures rise.

High clouds will continue to increase over the region Friday as the upper level ridge axis moves off to our east and a shortwave trough drifts over the desert Southwest. The ascent and vorticity enhancement with this disturbance will remain well to our south, and no precipitation is expected. However, cloud cover should keep temperatures a few degrees cooler, in the low to mid 60s at low elevations and 40s-50s for the mountains.

Temperatures finally cool down to near-average values for the time of year this weekend as a broad upper level trough (remnants of what was once a potent mid-latitude cyclone) slides southeast over our area. Areas of fog are likely to develop as far west as the I-25 corridor in the early morning hours Saturday as temperatures drop into the mid 30s and southerly winds, as well as a lee surface cyclone, advect higher dewpoints. The weakening upper level trough will also bring a plume of Pacific moisture that should promote light mountain snow and scattered rain showers over the plains Saturday afternoon. In terms of snow, 1 to 3 inches of total accumulation for this event seems reasonable at elevations above 10kft, with locally higher amounts above 12kft. For the low elevations, rain showers should remain quite light in intensity, with only a trace up to a few hundredths expected mainly over the east CO plains. A few snowflakes or a rain/snow mix cannot be ruled out over the Palmer Divide late Saturday evening as the system exits the region and temperatures begin to drop into the mid 30s.

Sunday is shaping up to be a mostly sunny autumn day with temperatures in the low to mid 50s for the Denver metro and east CO plains, which is near-average for the time of year. An upper level ridge will begin to build over our region on Sunday into Monday, with temperatures expected to warm back up into the 60s once again for much of the plains and foothills Monday-Tuesday. A pattern change is expected to arrive by Wednesday as a shortwave trough slides over northwest CO. This is also where uncertainty enters the picture, with ensemble guidance showing increasing spread in temperature and moisture through next weekend. At this time, our northern mountains look to be favored for mountain snow with the first wave on Wednesday. We are fairly confident in temperatures dropping to seasonable values by the end of next week. Long-range ensemble members and deterministic runs have continued to hint at another system bringing more mountain snow chances, and potentially some snow for the low elevations as well. However, it is far too early to come to any conclusions about snow amounts or even precipitation type. At this time, global model ensembles show a 15- degree spread in temperature between the 25th and 75th percentiles alone. Nevertheless, more active weather and cooler temperatures seem to be in store starting mid next week, likely continuing through Thanksgiving week.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Thursday...Fast southwest flow aloft develops again ahead of the closed low aloft across Idaho and Nevada.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue through Friday night.
- Chances of precipitation increase over the weekend for the mountains, but remain low for the plains.
- A more active pattern is expected into the middle of next week, with precipitation chances returning Wednesday into Thursday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Forecast remains on track into this weekend, so not many changes made to the previous forecast package with relatively quiet weather lingering through Sunday. This morning, surface observations and current 10.3-3.9 fog product loop shows low clouds and fog starting to roll into western Nebraska at this hour with Alliance now down to 4 miles VIS with low stratus near 400 feet AGL. Fog product shows this area of low clouds/fog slowly drifting westward and will likely impact most of western Nebraska, in some form, through 800 AM Friday morning...and may event impact Torrington and the lower elevations of Goshen and possibly Platte County by sunrise. Increased the coverage of fog to for most areas near and east of the Wyoming/Nebraska border this morning. Fog should lift and clear out between 8 and 10 AM. Not expecting persistent dense fog at this time, so may handle any locally dense fog with a Special Wx Statement early this morning if visibilities lower any more than a half mile.

For the rest of today (Friday), the high amplitude upper level ridge axis will move overhead this morning along with increasing high cloudiness. Should be a pleasant afternoon with high temperatures remaining in the upper 50s to mid 60s across most of the area, coolest temperatures could actually be over the western Nebraska panhandle depending on how quick the low clouds dissipate. Mildest temperatures will likely be located along and just east of the I-25 corridor.

For this weekend, models remain in good agreement, showing the next Pacific storm system moving across the Great Basin Region Friday night and gradually into the central Front Range on Saturday. With a dominate southern branch of the upper level jet, expect this system to split and likely remain south of us into Saturday night with the northern portion weakening over Montana. Another round of fog and/or low clouds likely across most of western Nebraska and far eastern Wyoming Friday night and early Saturday due to increasing upslope southeast winds ahead of this storm system, so continued to increase coverage of fog across the eastern half of the forecast area. Some precipitation can't be ruled out for the I-80 corridor, but chances are pretty low with maybe a few inches of snow for the Sierra Madre and Snowy Ranges Saturday evening. Temperatures will begin to lower on Saturday with a cooler airmass working its way into the region. High temperatures in the upper 40s to mid 50s expected due to cloud cover and upslope south to southeast winds. The Pacific storm system will gradually weaken and eject eastward on Sunday, leading to a slightly warmer day with dry conditions and light west to southwest winds.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Monday...The flow aloft backs to southwest, inducing surface lee troughing across our forecast area, and producing a continued warming trend as 700 mb temperatures rise to near 6 Celsius. Continued dry with limited low and mid level moisture.

Tuesday...Looks like a breezy to windy day as the flow aloft strengthens in advance of an approaching shortwave trough aloft from Utah and Arizona. Low and mid level moisture still looks too scant for any precipitation to reach the ground.

Wednesday...A progressive negatively tilted shortwave trough aloft will move across our counties, spreading chances for showers from west to east, with somewhat drier conditions by late afternoon in the wake of the shortwave trough aloft.

Thursday...Fast southwest flow aloft develops again ahead of the closed low aloft across Idaho and Nevada. Looks like enough synoptic and mesoscale lift and adequate moisture to produce showers spreading from west to east, until the late afternoon when subsidence behind the shortwave trough aloft will make it drier. 700 mb temperatures suggest temperatures will be somewhat similar when compared to Wednesday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A cooler and drier Sunday leads to a warmer Monday as ridging once again translates by as a stronger trough digs back upstream. The passage of this trough will brings another round of valley rain and mountain snow by mid week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions and above normal temperatures hang around for one more day before cooler conditions are ushered in.
- Valley rain and mountain snow returns to the forecast this weekend favoring the southern mountains and adjacent foothills.
- After a quiet start to the week an active weather pattern set up for much of next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: This evening's H500 hand analysis map has a highly amplified ridge over the Rockies...extending through central Canada and across Hudson Bay. The ridge is being flanked by a large digging downstream trough over the East and a pair of upstream cyclones over the EPac approaching the coastline. The ridge will translate to the High Plains tomorrow and br further squeezed between the two troughs but it's influence and the southerly flow ahead of the upstream system will keep another mild day in place. Highs will generally be around 5 to 10 degrees above normal even with mid to high cloudiness drifting through.
COOLER, WETTER CHANGE HEADING INTO THE WEEKEND:

Water vapor shows a lead system being kicked toward the Baja this evening by a much stronger cyclone dropping out of the Gulf of AK. A weak AR associated with this southern system will allow the first influx of moisture to be pulled across the 4 Corners on southerly flow as early as tomorrow morning...though the bulk of it will be remain well to the South. This moisture will be more of a primer for a stronger push of moisture moving in tomorrow night. A moderate AR is associated with the northern cyclone which will be impinging upon the Sierras through much of tomorrow as it drops southward. As it drops across the southern flank of the upstream terrain IVT suggests we get a more robust push of moisture into our eastern and southern CWA by late tomorrow evening. Don't expect much in accumulating precipitation until this secondary moisture arrives though some high elevation orographics snow showers and sprinkles in the lower elevations could be possible by sunset. Luckily this system is not brining the highly anomalous moisture as the past few and even though it drops in negatively tilted...will be short lived. Though not overly cold much of the precipitation above 8500-9000 feet should locked in as snow. The persistent moist southerly flow will allow the southern San Juans to once again catch the best precipitation for the event. Other ranges will do better Saturday morning and early afternoon as the front passes through and the overall dynamics aloft are the strongest. Snow levels hover around 9K before fropa then drop to mountain bases by sunset as the storm is exiting. Storm totals of 4-10 inches are most likely over the southern San Juans above 9K with ensemble spot forecasts suggesting higher amounts near a foot in a few favored locations. A bigger challenge is forecasting possible impacts as much of the snow should melt as it hits the roadways during the daylight hours...leaving only a few hours of slushy/snowpacked roads near sunrise on Saturday and over the northern passes after sunset before the system exits. For now will continue to hold off on any winter highlights with other mountain locations only seeing a few inches at best. The liquid precipitation forecast across the lower elevation basins of the San Juan River remain in the quarter to half inch range as the highest probability outcome and hydrographs show only minimal responses at this point.

A cooler and drier Sunday leads to a warmer Monday as ridging once again translates by as a stronger trough digs back upstream. The passage of this trough will brings another round of valley rain and mountain snow by mid week. IVT forecasts suggest a more robust push of moisture and QPF amounts increase as a result. Unsettled conditions persist into the end of the week as low pressure looks to take over much of the West. Forecast confidence is very low at this time due to differences in the timing, strength, and track of this late week system.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Looking at the Statistical DESI guidance, over 4 feet of snow is forecast for the Wolf Creek area during the next 10 days.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Another nice day today although it will be a few degrees cooler than yesterday.
- Snow moves into the San Juans this evening, with heaviest precip tomorrow morning, precip decreasing later in the afternoon.
- Shower over the plains saturday, best chance late Saturday over far SE CO. SNOW (light accums) is possible N El Paso county Saturday evening.
- Dry from later Sunday into midday Tuesday.
- Another mountain snow event late Tuesday into Wednesday.
- Unsettled late week as a LARGE Pacific trough closes off over the California region. Significant mtn snows likely (eventually) as strong trough moves east over intermountain west.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: As quiet as the last week was weatherwise, this upcoming week will likely be the opposite. The ridge which has been over the region will be replaced a series of Pacific storm systems that will move over the region starting tonight and lasting into next week(end).

For the immediate short term, we will likely see some fog over the eastern plains tonight as cooler air moves over the plains and low level moisture increases. Fog could reach as far east a KPUB, but the brunt of it will be over the US-50 corridor from Pueblo east, and also over most of Prowers and Baca counties.
For today, one more mild day is likely, although it will be a few degrees cooler today than yesterday. Clouds will steadily increase over the region as the day progresses.

Snow showers will move into the San Juans this evening, with the precip gradually picking up as the night progresses, Snow levels will likely be at 9000 feet, gradually decreasing below 9000 feet by Sunrise.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: For Saturday, snow will fall across the mountains with snow levels in the 8000's through the day, with values slowly decreasing as the day progresses. Heaviest precip will occur Saturday morning across the eastern San Juan mountains, with the precip decreasing later in the day. A total of 4 to 7 inches of snow will be likely above 9000 feet.

It will be cloudy over the entire region Saturday and it will be noticeably cooler region-wide. It will become rather windy (south winds) over the far eastern plains. Showers will develop over the I- 25 corridor by mid morning with the activity pushing onto the eastern plains later in the day. The storm system is expected to wrap up somewhat as it moves over the plains, and this will allow for some heavier precip to occur over the far southeast plains late in the day and into the evening hours.
As the storm wraps up, cooler air will spread southward on the backside of the system, and we may see some light accumulations of snow across N El Paso county Saturday evening.

Sunday...any showers over the eastern plains will push into KS by late morning. Otherwise it will dry out with sun returning to the region. It will be cool Sunday with mainly temps around 50 over the plains and valleys.
Monday...Sunny and mild with highs in the 50s plains/valleys.

Tuesday...Mild once again with 60s returning to the plains, mid 50s valleys. Another strong Pacific trough will move towards the region. This system is a fairly stout mid level trough but it will move over us as an open wave, and most of the forcing will stay to the north and west of us. Nonetheless, west to southwest mid level moist flow will bring snows to mainly the Continental Divide region, and several inches of wind driven snow will be likely, especially Tuesday night into early Wednesday.

For late next week, a rather very impressive trough is forecast to move into the western United States. A large trough is forecast to move in from the Pacific Northwest and then close off over the greater central California area by late Friday. Moist southwest flow will gradually develop over the 4 corners and snow will once again develop over the CONTDVD region by late week. This circulation is then forecast to move slowly east-southeast with time.
Looking at the Statistical DESI guidance, over 4 feet of snow is forecast for the Wolf Creek area during the next 10 days.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: After a brief break Wednesday into Wednesday night, yet another storm system could impact the area by Thursday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions will give way to widespread valley rain and mountain snow late Friday into Saturday.

- Two more storms arrive next week with the first on Tuesday/Wednesday that looks very similar to the Saturday storm, and another towards the end of the week that has high-end scenario potential, but run-to-run consistency has been lacking.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A high-amplitude ridge has shifted east of Utah into Colorado this evening while upstream, a couple of storm systems are noted on water vapor satellite imagery. One is a closed low off the SoCal coast, while a second, larger, closed low is approaching the PacNW. The southern low will be coming onshore near the Cal/Baja coast by midday Friday. This system will gradually weaken as it becomes absorbed into the southerlies that will strengthen ahead of the second storm, which will continue to make its way onto the PacNW coast on Friday. The two storms will eventually phase into a negatively tilted trough which will then cross Utah Friday night through Saturday.

Given the increased southerly flow, some moisture will spread north into Utah on Friday ahead of the southern stream storm. As such, expect isolated to scattered showers to develop Friday afternoon into Friday evening. This will take place under a relatively mild airmass, with snow levels remaining mostly above 8500 ft during this timeframe. Precipitation will then become more widespread Friday night through Saturday morning ahead of and with a relatively fast-moving cold front. Snow levels will quickly fall to around 6-7 kft by around midday Saturday. However, precipitation will mostly wind down by late morning or midday Saturday behind the cold front, with the exception of the mountains, particularly those areas favored in northwesterly flow, which will maintain brief orographics into the afternoon. Additionally, with warm temperatures over the GSL, expect some showers to continue developing of the lake into the central Wasatch Front and adjacent mountains as well.

Most valleys are expected to see storm total precipitation amounts between 0.4-0.7 inches near the I-15 corridor and less elsewhere. Meanwhile, mountains are expected to see 0.6-1.2 inches with locally higher amounts in the upper Cottonwoods and near Brian Head. Snow amounts remain generally in the 4-8 inch range, mainly above 7500 feet, with higher amounts possible in the upper Cottonwoods, Tushars, and near Brian Head.

A transient ridge will cross the area late Saturday through Monday, bringing a break in the weather. However, the pattern remains progressive, with the next storm system looking to impact the area during the Monday night through Tuesday night timeframe. This will be another relatively fast-moving system which will also bring widespread precipitation to the area. However, it looks like this could be a colder system, which will result in lower snow levels, potentially down to at least 5000 feet.

After a brief break Wednesday into Wednesday night, yet another storm system could impact the area by Thursday morning. There is good agreement in the large-scale pattern regarding the existence of this late week storm, but with uncertainties in the timing and evolution. Latest global deterministics are leaning towards this storm being a broad closed low which will slowly move through the region through the weekend, bringing an extended period of precipitation to the forecast area.

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Chris Dickson
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. Avoid isolated pockets of wind-drifted snow above treeline. Expect danger to rise going into the weekend as new snowfall stacks up on Saturday.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel, with too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow below ridges or in gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: You can expect generally safe avalanche conditions. The few spots where you may be able to trigger a slab avalanche are where you find wind-drifted snow on slopes facing the north half of the compass above treeline. Look for small cornices above a slope, or stiffer, smooth snow surface to illustrate any steep spots to avoid.
